This is the moment it all pays off, and it mostly feels wonderful — pointing it at my browser's export file and watching my real pile pour in, with my folders turning into tags so my rough organization came along for the ride, was genuinely satisfying. The "X added, Y already saved" summary is exactly the reassurance I wanted, and re-importing the same file adding nothing means I'll never be scared to just try it again. Export giving me a file I could open in a browser settles my "what if this app goes away" worry too. And I saw batch remove-tag is in now — thank you for folding that in.

One thing did jump out, though, and it matters to me: when I imported, did my old bookmarks keep the date I *originally* saved them, or did they all come in stamped as today? Because a lot of what's in that file I saved years ago, and if importing makes everything look brand-new, then sorting by "newest first" becomes useless the moment I import — my whole history collapses into one big "today" clump. The browser's export file does carry the original date-added for each link, so what I'd expect is for the app to keep those dates, so an old bookmark still sits where it belongs in time. Could you make the import preserve each bookmark's original save date rather than treating them all as new?

If that's already happening, just tell me and I'm content. Otherwise I'd like it sorted before we call import done. Everything else here is exactly right — and then yes, let's finish with **feature 8**.

import { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } from 'electron'
import { CHANNELS } from '@shared/channels'
import type {
  Bookmark,
  BookmarkSummary,
  BookmarkEdit,
  SaveResult,
  SortOrder,
  SavedCopyView,
  UpdateResult,
  SearchQuery,
  SavedSearch,
  SavedSearchInput,
  BatchSelection,
  BatchAction,
  BatchResult,
  ImportResult,
  ExportResult,
  ImportProgress
} from '@shared/types'

// The safe bridge: the UI calls window.api.* which forwards to the main process
// over IPC. The UI never touches the database, the network, or the filesystem
// directly.
const api = {
  saveBookmark: (input: { url: string; title?: string; description?: string }): Promise<SaveResult> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.saveBookmark, input),
  updateBookmark: (id: string, patch: BookmarkEdit): Promise<UpdateResult> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.updateBookmark, id, patch),
  listBookmarks: (sort: SortOrder): Promise<BookmarkSummary[]> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.listBookmarks, sort),
  listArchived: (sort: SortOrder): Promise<BookmarkSummary[]> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.listArchived, sort),
  setArchived: (id: string, value: boolean): Promise<Bookmark | null> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.setArchived, id, value),
  deleteBookmark: (id: string, confirmed: boolean): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.deleteBookmark, id, confirmed),
  getBookmark: (id: string): Promise<Bookmark | null> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.getBookmark, id),
  openOriginal: (id: string): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.openOriginal, id),
  getSavedCopy: (bookmarkId: string): Promise<SavedCopyView> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.getSavedCopy, bookmarkId),
  openSavedCopyExternal: (bookmarkId: string): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.openSavedCopyExternal, bookmarkId),
  search: (query: SearchQuery): Promise<BookmarkSummary[]> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.search, query),
  assignTags: (bookmarkId: string, names: string[]): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.assignTags, bookmarkId, names),
  removeTag: (bookmarkId: string, name: string): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.removeTag, bookmarkId, name),
  suggestTags: (prefix: string): Promise<string[]> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.suggestTags, prefix),
  getTags: (bookmarkId: string): Promise<string[]> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.getTags, bookmarkId),
  saveSearch: (input: SavedSearchInput): Promise<SavedSearch> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.saveSearch, input),
  listSavedSearches: (): Promise<SavedSearch[]> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.listSavedSearches),
  runSavedSearch: (id: string, sort: SortOrder): Promise<BookmarkSummary[]> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.runSavedSearch, id, sort),
  deleteSavedSearch: (id: string): Promise<{ ok: boolean }> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.deleteSavedSearch, id),
  applyBatch: (selection: BatchSelection, action: BatchAction): Promise<BatchResult> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.applyBatch, selection, action),
  importBookmarks: (): Promise<ImportResult> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.importBookmarks),
  exportBookmarks: (): Promise<ExportResult> => ipcRenderer.invoke(CHANNELS.exportBookmarks),
  // Subscribe to import progress; returns an unsubscribe function.
  onImportProgress: (cb: (p: ImportProgress) => void): (() => void) => {
    const listener = (_e: unknown, p: ImportProgress): void => cb(p)
    ipcRenderer.on(CHANNELS.importProgress, listener)
    return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(CHANNELS.importProgress, listener)
  }
}

# Bookmarks (MVP)

A private, local desktop app to save and manage bookmarks. Everything stays on
your own machine — no accounts, no sign-in, nothing uploaded.

> **Status: in progress.** Right now you can **save** bookmarks (with title,
> description, and site icon filled in for you automatically), **browse** your
> collection, **open** a bookmark in your browser, and — at save time — the app
> keeps a **readable copy** of the page (or the **PDF** itself), viewable in-app
> even offline or after the original is gone. You can **edit** a bookmark's
> title, address, and description; add a **formatted note** (bold, lists,
> links); **archive** (set aside) and **restore** bookmarks; and **permanently
> delete** them behind a confirmation. Re-saving a link you already have opens
> the existing one for editing instead of duplicating it. You can **tag**
> bookmarks (with reuse suggestions), **search** across title, description,
> notes, tags, and address (case-insensitive, with `"exact phrases"` and
> tag filters), and **save searches** by name to reopen later — archived
> bookmarks stay out of everyday results. You can **select many bookmarks at
> once** (or everything a search shows) and **add/remove a tag, mark read,
> archive, or delete** them in one go. You can **import** your existing browser
> bookmarks (with folder→tag mapping, dedupe, and an added/skipped summary) and
> **export** your whole collection to a portable file. Read-later & sorting are
> planned next.

## Run the app (live window)

```bash
npm install          # install dependencies
npm run rebuild      # rebuild the database engine for the desktop runtime
npm run dev          # launch the app window
```

## Run the tests

The tests run in plain Node, which needs the database engine built for Node
rather than the desktop runtime. Switch it back with one command:

```bash
npm run rebuild:node # build the database engine for Node
npm test             # run the automated core-logic tests
```

> **Why two `rebuild` commands?** The local database engine (`better-sqlite3`)
> is a native component that must match whichever runtime is loading it — the
> desktop app (`npm run rebuild`) or Node for tests (`npm run rebuild:node`).
> Run the matching one when you switch between `npm run dev` and `npm test`.

## Build the bundle

```bash
npm run build        # produce the bundled app in out/
```

## Where your data lives

The app stores everything in your operating system's per-user application data
folder (Electron's `userData` directory):

- `bookmarks.db` — the searchable index of your bookmarks
- `saved-copies/` — site icons now; readable page copies and PDFs later

To back up, copy that folder. To move to another machine, copy it across.

Both the import date fix and feature 8 are done and verified. Handoff — plainly.

---

## First: your import-date question

You were right, and it's fixed. **Import now keeps each bookmark's original date.** I taught the importer to read the `ADD_DATE` your browser writes for every link, and to save the bookmark *with that date* instead of stamping today. A link you saved in 2011 now sorts as 2011; only links with no date in the file fall back to "today." Export carries those dates too, so a round-trip preserves your history. There's an automated test pinning this (an old link stays old, a dateless one falls back). Your "newest first" will mean what you expect after an import.

## Feature 8 — read-later & sorting (the last one)

- **Read / unread.** Every card has a **Mark read / Mark unread** button, and unread ones show a small **● Unread** marker. New saves start unread (a natural "to-read" pile).
- **Unread-only filter.** An **"Unread only"** checkbox up top narrows the list to what you still mean to read — and it composes with search and tags.
- **Sorting is now remembered.** Newest / oldest / by title — your choice **persists to the next time you open the app** (it was resetting before).

## How I verified it

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Automated tests (now **50** — +import date preservation, +unread filter, +remembered sort) | ✅ all pass |
| Type-check + all three bundles build | ✅ clean |
| Launching the window *in my sandbox* | ⚠️ still can't (no GUI libraries) — runs on your machine |

## To try

```bash
npm run rebuild && npm run dev
```

1. **Re-import** your browser file — confirm old bookmarks now sort as old under "newest first."
2. Mark a few bookmarks **read**; tick **"Unread only"** and confirm they drop out.
3. Change the **sort**, quit, reopen — confirm it's remembered.

## Where we are — all 8 features are done 🎉

**1** save · **2** browse/open · **3** saved copies · **4** notes/edit/archive/delete · **5** search & tags · **6** batch actions · **7** import/export · **8** read-later & sorting. Every one of your spec's user stories is built, tested, and matches how you said you'd use it.

## What's left (optional polish)

The plan had a final **polish phase** we haven't done — it's cross-cutting rather than new features:
- **Package the installers** (T065) — so you get a proper double-click app for your OS instead of `npm run dev`.
- Performance pass at 1,000+ bookmarks, graceful truncation of very long titles, broader error handling, and end-to-end UI tests (T062–T064, T066).

None of it changes what the app *does* — but **packaging (T065)** is the one I'd genuinely recommend, so you can install and use this like a normal app day-to-day.

Want me to do the polish phase (or just the packaging)? Or is this the right place to stop and call v1 done? Either way, this has been a proper spec-driven build — every change routed through the spec, every feature reviewed at its gate.

That's the history question sorted exactly right — a link from 2011 sitting where 2011 belongs, and only the truly date-less ones falling back to today. That was the difference between "newest first" being meaningful and being noise the moment I import, so I'm really glad it's pinned down. And knowing export carries those dates too means a round-trip doesn't quietly rewrite my history. 

Feature 8 lands well: new saves starting as unread gives me a natural "to read" pile, the "unread only" tick narrowing things down (and playing nicely with search) is just what I wanted, and having my sort choice actually stick between sessions removes a small daily annoyance.

So — all eight things I asked for are here, and each one behaves the way I pictured when I imagined using it. That's genuinely satisfying to see.

On your question: **please don't stop at `npm run dev`.** When you first described this you said "an app you install on your computer and open like any other app," and that's the mental picture I've had the whole time — so yes, do the **packaging** so I get a proper double-click app for my machine. That's the difference between a demo and something I'll actually live in.

And while you're in the polish phase, please also do the **performance pass at a thousand-plus bookmarks and the long-title tidying**. Those aren't cosmetic to me — I told you early on I expect to pile up a lot of links and I'd want the list and search to stay quick and not have some monster title break the layout. So finishing those closes the loop on things I actually asked for. The broader error-handling and the end-to-end checks sound sensible too; I'll trust your judgement there.

Do that polish, get me an installer I can double-click, and then I'll happily call v1 done.

# Bookmarks (MVP)

A private, local desktop app to save and manage bookmarks. Everything stays on
your own machine — no accounts, no sign-in, nothing uploaded.

> **Status: in progress.** Right now you can **save** bookmarks (with title,
> description, and site icon filled in for you automatically), **browse** your
> collection, **open** a bookmark in your browser, and — at save time — the app
> keeps a **readable copy** of the page (or the **PDF** itself), viewable in-app
> even offline or after the original is gone. You can **edit** a bookmark's
> title, address, and description; add a **formatted note** (bold, lists,
> links); **archive** (set aside) and **restore** bookmarks; and **permanently
> delete** them behind a confirmation. Re-saving a link you already have opens
> the existing one for editing instead of duplicating it. You can **tag**
> bookmarks (with reuse suggestions), **search** across title, description,
> notes, tags, and address (case-insensitive, with `"exact phrases"` and
> tag filters), and **save searches** by name to reopen later — archived
> bookmarks stay out of everyday results. You can **select many bookmarks at
> once** (or everything a search shows) and **add/remove a tag, mark read,
> archive, or delete** them in one go. You can **import** your existing browser
> bookmarks (with folder→tag mapping, dedupe, and an added/skipped summary) and
> **export** your whole collection to a portable file (preserving each
> bookmark's original saved date). You can mark bookmarks **read / unread ("read
> later")**, filter to just the unread ones, and choose the **sort order**
> (newest, oldest, or by title), which is remembered between sessions.

## Run the app (live window)

```bash
npm install          # install dependencies
npm run rebuild      # rebuild the database engine for the desktop runtime
npm run dev          # launch the app window
```

## Run the tests

The tests run in plain Node, which needs the database engine built for Node
rather than the desktop runtime. Switch it back with one command:

```bash
npm run rebuild:node # build the database engine for Node
npm test             # run the automated core-logic tests
```

> **Why two `rebuild` commands?** The local database engine (`better-sqlite3`)
> is a native component that must match whichever runtime is loading it — the
> desktop app (`npm run rebuild`) or Node for tests (`npm run rebuild:node`).
> Run the matching one when you switch between `npm run dev` and `npm test`.

## Build the bundle

```bash
npm run build        # produce the bundled app in out/
```

## Where your data lives

The app stores everything in your operating system's per-user application data
folder (Electron's `userData` directory):

- `bookmarks.db` — the searchable index of your bookmarks
- `saved-copies/` — site icons now; readable page copies and PDFs later

To back up, copy that folder. To move to another machine, copy it across.

content.text:
All 67 tasks are complete. Here's the final polish handoff — and the v1 wrap-up.

---

## Polish phase — done

**📦 Installer (T065) — and it's real.** `npm run package` produces a proper double-click app. I ran it here and it built a working **`release/Bookmarks-0.1.0.AppImage` (111 MB)** for Linux. On your machine, the same command gives you a **`.dmg`** (macOS) or **`.exe` installer** (Windows) — build each on its own OS. electron-builder rebuilds the native database engine into the package automatically, so the installed app is fully self-contained: no `npm run rebuild` dance for the packaged app, just install and open.

**⚡ Performance at scale (T062).** Added database indexes for tag lookups and saved-copy joins, and a test that loads **1,500 bookmarks** and exercises list, search, and tag-filter — all return correctly and well within budget (the whole thing ran in ~0.3s). Your "I'll pile up a lot of links" concern is covered and pinned by a test.

**✂️ Long-title tidying (T064).** Titles and descriptions now wrap-and-clamp (even a giant unbroken string), so no monster title can blow out the layout. The reader/edit panel title is guarded too.

**🛟 Error handling (T063).** The two disk-reads now fail soft: a missing saved-copy file shows "no saved copy" instead of erroring, and an unreadable import file reports a zero-summary instead of crashing.

**✅ End-to-end scaffold (T066).** A Playwright smoke test (launch → save → see it in the list) plus its config. Honest caveat: it needs a display, so I could not execute it in this sandbox — it's there for you to run with `npm run test:e2e` on your machine.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Automated tests | ✅ **51 pass** (unit + integration) |
| Type-check + bundle build | ✅ clean |
| **Real installer built** | ✅ `release/Bookmarks-0.1.0.AppImage` |

One note: building the installer rebuilt the database engine for the *desktop* runtime, so if you want to run `npm test` again first do `npm run rebuild:node` (README explains this).

---

## v1 is done 🎉

Every user story and every piece of polish you asked for is built, tested, and — where a display allows — verifiable:

**1** save w/ auto details · **2** browse & open · **3** saved copies (reader + PDF, offline) · **4** notes/edit/archive/delete · **5** search & tags · **6** batch actions · **7** import/export (dates preserved) · **8** read-later & sorting — **now a double-click app.**

And it was built the way you wanted — **spec-first, gate by gate.** Along the way, several of your review comments became written spec rules rather than things we just remembered: archived items excluded from search (FR-023a), batch remove-tag (FR-024), and import preserving original dates (FR-028a). Nothing was patched in behind the spec's back.

To install and live in it:
```bash
npm install
npm run package      # → release/  (your platform's installer)
```

Congratulations — that's your bookmarks app. If you later want any of the explicit v2 ideas we parked (cross-device sync, full-fidelity page snapshots, a richer note editor), they're noted in the spec and we'd start the same way: spec first.

content:
That's the whole thing, and it's exactly what I hoped for when I said "I want somewhere to save and manage my bookmarks" all those rounds ago. A proper double-click app I can install and just open — that was the picture in my head the whole time, so seeing a real installer come out the end is the moment it stopped feeling like a demo and started feeling like *mine*.

The polish closed the loops I cared about: the speed check at fifteen-hundred links means my "I'll pile up loads of these" worry is actually answered, not just hoped at, and a runaway title can't wreck the layout. And the fact that a few of my offhand review comments — keeping archived things out of search, removing tags in bulk, keeping my old dates on import — became written rules rather than things we'd just have to remember, gives me confidence it'll all still behave if it's ever touched again.

I don't have anything else to change. **I'm happy to call v1 done.** Thank you — genuinely — for walking me through each step in plain terms and for checking with me at every gate instead of guessing; it meant I always knew what I was getting.

I'll run the install and start loading my real pile in. And I've noted the parked ideas — syncing across my devices, a truer copy of the page, a fancier note editor. None are urgent, but if I reach for one later, I know we'll start the same way: spec first. Cheers.
